Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to be able to address myself to Bill C-4 which is before us this afternoon relating to grants to municipalities. I have listened with a great deal of interest to all of the speakers, and 1 concur with the points of view raised. I feel it would not be appropriate for me simply to repeat what has already been said in the spirit of moving hastily to ensure the speedy
Grants to Municipalities
passage of this bill and getting it into committee where it will be examined in detail. I have confidence that the minister will receive our comments well and see that the suggested improvements to the bill in fact take place.
There are two items, however, which I would like to mention specifically to emphasize the fact that the bill does not recognize seriously the differences in municipalities across the country. Certain municipalities will receive benefits far in excess of benefits received elsewhere simply because of the nature of the taxation base in these various municipalities.
I must also stress the need for some consideration of payment a bit earlier than what has traditionally been the case.
As a member of a city council for a number of years I can say that it was always a disappointment when we had to wait so long to receive the moneys we expected from the federal government. This caused a great deal of uncertainty and concern about the ability of the municipality to pay its bills and meet its obligations in terms of providing services to its taxpayers.
The city I represented as a city council member certainly recognized that there are many, many problems facing municipalities today, not the least of which are financial problems. We found ourselves in a situation where we had to go out and borrow money. At that time we were borrowing from foreign sources, and very shortly thereafter, because of the rapid devaluation of the Canadian dollar, we found ourselves in a situation where we had to be paying off huge foreign debts in terms of Swiss francs, German marks or American dollars. This simply added to the financial problems of the municipality.
This bill is certainly a step in the right direction but, as the minister responsible indicated, it does not go far enough. There are many problems this bill does not address. In this form, of course, it cannot address them. It is not a panacea for all the problems that face municipalities today but a step in the right direction. 1 suggest it is a small step in the right direction, especially when one considers the major jump backwards that was taken in 1978 when the Liberal government at the time did away with the department of urban affairs, a move which was, in a sense, supported by the Conservative party in their brief time in office.
I suggest that more than ever before there is a need for more active leadership to be shown by the federal government in terms of urban development and municipal affairs. When confederation came into being more than 100 years ago, the composition of our population was significantly different from what it is today. At that time 80 per cent of the population was rural and only 20 per cent was urban. Today we find the situation completely reversed; 80 per cent of Canadians live in urban areas and 20 per cent live in rural areas. Perhaps we could even make a strong case for saying that those living in the so-called rural areas, small villages and towns, are in fact urban dwellers as well and face many of the problems, stresses and challenges of the urban dwellers. One can make a case
1214

May 20, 1980
Grants to Municipalities
that 90 per cent of Canada's population today is experiencing urban difficulties and problems. Maybe this bill is the beginning of that process and maybe this is the time for the federal government to demonstrate serious leadership in terms of urban and municipal affairs, to provide the initiative which is presently lacking in many parts of the country.
Many of our provincial governments bear the responsibility for some of the shortcomings. I must say that I feel the federal government, relative to some of the provincial governments, has done an admirable job. However, a great deal of work is yet to be done, a great deal of creativity and innovation is before us, and that opportunity is certainly knocking at a time when scarce public funds require optimum and efficient use, where cost effective measures have never been as needed as they are today. It is a time for the federal government to provide creative, energetic initiative and leadership in Canada when it comes to dealing with urban challenges.
We see a country-and we are reminded of it especially today-of extreme diversity. Yet when you look at the nature of the cities, towns and villages across this diverse country, you recognize that similar problems exist there. The fact that a municipality may be 3,000 miles away does not necessarily mean that it shares different problems in terms of the servicing of expensive suburbs or in terms of experiencing crises in rental accommodation or perhaps vacancy rates in the neighbourhood of 1 per cent, or in some cases down to 0.1 per cent or 0.2 per cent, where housing construction, particularly social housing, is a major challenge facing both large and mediumsized municipalities, providing for expensive urban infrastructure of all sorts, sewage systems, road systems, parks, and so on.
In the whole matter of urban transportation, be it public transportation, rapid transportation, on the kinds of problems that face municipalities from one end of this country to another, the municipalities are left on their own. Either because they have to resort to the private sector or make use of various consulting firms, or essentially have to reinvent the wheel, they are not taking advantage of the experience of sister municipalities in other parts of the country. They are not taking advantage of the experience which other municipalities have had in providing services and recognizing the difficulties which others have already experienced.
It seems that here is an opportunity for us as the federal government to play a role in providing a type of clearing house, in providing a kind of co-operative energy to bring to bear the existing knowledge, expertise and information that many municipalities and many urban centres would enjoy and from which they would benefit. It would save them the expense of finding what they think are unique solutions when, in fact, a few miles away there might be old solutions.
1 feel that the challenge of energy cost to municipalities is something which the federal government must address in terms of providing leadership. The municipality which 1 had the privilege of serving in the past used to expend, a handful of years ago, $50,000 on their hydro charges to pump water to the various parts of the city. In a handful of years, that
amount of money has changed from $50,000 to nearly one-third of a million dollars. The responsibility for that was borne, by and large, at the local level in terms of meeting those servicing costs.
With regard to cultural opportunities, we are seeing a great deal of initiative taken now in various communities across the country, initiative which we must nurture, encourage and support, where communities are coming together and building small community centres, theatres, art galleries, facilities to welcome and provide a home for the visual and performing arts, something which, if we are to weld this fine country together in a spirit which every member in the House would like to see, we should encourage.
Again this is another apportunity for the federal government to provide leadership and to show the way, through funding and, perhaps as important, through providing the co-operative energy of bringing together people and ideas to find a solution to these problems. However, we have seen in the past a cutting back in that leadership, a reduction in the leadership where the federal government, in an attempt perhaps to be more cost efficient through the consolidation of various federal programs and the transference of those consolidated programs into the provincial sphere, has given the provinces more responsibility in distributing federal funds.
One has to reflect on whether or not that has always resulted in a better service and a better opportunity for people dwelling in municipalities. For example, the urban transportation assistance program provided the initiative for programs such as railroad relocation to be transferred from the sphere of the federal government to that of the provincial government. Sums of money were made available to assist in urban transportation, which caught a number of municipalities part way along their own planning of expenditures to relocate outmoded and problematic rail transportation yards from the central part of the city to the outskirts. Once the provinces had the ability to decide how those funds might be expended, based perhaps in some cases on their own political motivation, and they chose not to continue a number of those programs, much to the disappointment of those municipalities which had already expended significant sums of money, the municipalities were left holding the bag.
When one considers that leadership in terms of our urban centres is required as it never was before, where a clearing house for information and ideas could be provided by the federal government, one recognizes the importance of our request to the minister that he reconsider, in his time in office, the decision to abandon the department of urban affairs and rethink the role that it could play in a country which is, by and large, urban. This is one of the most urban countries in the entire world.
In closing, let me comment, Mr. Speaker, on another matter which I feel must be addressed. This is the problem which faces virtually all municipalities, both large and small, across our country. It is the whole matter of the preservation of the quality of our environment.
May 20, 1980

We in Canada are fortunate to be one of those countries which by and large has a clean environment that must be preserved. Yet this clean environment, particularly as it affects our waterways, is being placed in jeopardy almost on a daily basis as municipalities attempt to deal with their sewage disposal problems more often than not in not very creative ways, limited by the amount of funding that is available to them, and as a consequence placing many of our streams, rivers and coastal areas in jeopardy.
1 should like to take this opportunity to use as an example the city of Kamloops which is in my riding. It is a city with a population of about 65,000 people. It has traditionally used a sewage lagoon method to treat sewage and then drain the essentially treated effluent into the river system. As the population has increased so rapidly over the past few years with growth rates in excess of 10 per cent, the present system reached its capacity in 1976. With major heavy industrial developments being proposed over the next year or two, we can see a greater and greater strain being placed on our river system, especially the ecology of that very sensitive system.
It is clear that to continue this way would be tantamount to catastrophe in terms of the delicate ecological base of our river system. The cost for an improvement of that system ranges somewhere in the neighbourhood of between $20 million and $90 million for a municipality of 65,000 votes. 1 suggest that that is placing an unrealistic responsibility on that municipality. I simply use it as an example because the same could be applied to municipalities, large and small, across the country. The $20 million cost would be the cheapest solution, and that is a continuation of the status quo; $90 million would provide an efficient and effective long-term solution which would take the effluent from that city and deposit it, using a land disposal method.
Of course, one of the major problems is not so much the polluting of the river system per se, but the fact that the Thompson River, a tributary of the Fraser River in British Columbia, perhaps is one of the most productive salmon fishery rivers in Canada. Not only is it a system that is part of the salmon migratory route, but it also has very crucial and important salmon spawning grounds. Therefore, it is crucial not only to the salmon industry of the Thompson and Fraser Rivers, but the Gulf of Georgia and indeed the Pacific Ocean itself. We are looking here at a renewable resource in excess of $300 million for the salmon fishery alone. I feel it is something that we must recognize. It is an area where the federal government, through its funding agencies, could play a very significant leadership role in providing the much needed relief.
In closing, may 1 say that I am very encouraged by the remarks of the previous speakers this afternoon. 1 am very pleased to see that so much work has gone into a bill in terms of identifying many of its shortcomings. I am optimistic, with proposals like those regarding the reinstatement of tri-level conferences, that perhaps this is a small step, a beginning, toward the leadership role so dearly required at this time.

speechtext:
that Bill C-202, to amend the Federal Court Act (disclosure of documents), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I wish to make only a few comments with regard to my bill, which seeks to amend the Federal
Court Act by deleting subsection (2) of section 41 of the said act.
Over the last few months, as you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members of the House know, we have been very much preoccupied with the debate which would lead us to greater freedom of information in this country. Indeed, the former government had a bill before the House which was initiated and sponsored mainly by our former colleague, the former hon. member for Peace River.
The term "freedom of information" is to be defined as meaning information held by government and kept secret; in other words, information that is not available to private citizens.
All of us agree that excessive government secrecy is in no way consistent with the most basic rights and fundamental principles of a society such as we espouse ours to be. The private individual does not like his or her government to keep information about him or her which could later on affect him or her in his or her career, relationships with government or, indeed, relationship with friends and neighbours. I will have something to say a little later by way of giving some practical examples of how excessive secrecy can affect individuals in our society.
Information selectively released by a government can, and I am sure has in the past-perhaps not deliberately-frustrate the orderly process of elections, and it certainly has from time to time influenced the judgment of voters when a government has had certain information that was not available to all the electors and has chosen to release that information selectively.
My bill, C-202, speaks of a different kind of secrecy or executive privilege, namely, information which is held by the government and may be withheld from the courts, or from the judiciary, under section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act.
I am a layman, not a lawyer, and at times I consider myself fortunate in not having had any legal training. In the words of a very renowned law professor, that might have sharpened my mind to the point where it would be so narrow I would not be able to comprehend what goes on in the rest of the world around me. Why should I as a layman raise this matter when over half of our friends and colleagues in the House of Commons are lawyers? I have pondered this question from time to time. Nevertheless, I am taking the initiative in raising this matter in the form of a private member's bill and I will give my reasons.
I have been startled as I progressed with my research by the fact that so little attention was paid to this bill when it was introduced in the House of Commons. Government members dealt with it rather flippantly, and I must say that my learned friends on this side of the House in the opposition as well paid very little attention to it. The debate was very short and very reserved. In fact, when the bill got to committee there was no great outcry from members of the legal profession that section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act could in some way seriously restrict the rights and freedoms of individuals in our society.
May 20, 1980

The Federal Court Act received Royal Assent on December 3, 1970 and came into force on June 1, 1971. Generally section 41(1) provides that if a minister certifies to a court that a document should not be released on grounds of public interest, the court may still examine the document and order its release. Subsection (2), however, gives the minister absolute right to refuse disclosure of documents which he certifies would be injurious to international relations, national defence or security, federal-provincial relations, or confidences of the Privy Council, without any examination by the court.
This is a provision in our Federal Court Act which is unique in the western world. There is not another country in the western world that has built this kind of a privilege into a federal court act. Let me quote section 41 with its two subsections. It is short and this will not take too much time. It states:
41. (1) Subject to the provisions of any other act and to subsection (2), when a minister of the Crown certifies to any court by affidavit that a document belongs to a class or contains information which on grounds of a public interest specified in the affidavit should be withheld from production and discovery, the court may examine the document and order its production and discovery to the parties, subject to such restrictions or conditions as it deems appropriate, if it concludes in the circumstances of the case that the public interest in the proper administration of justice outweighs in importance the public interest specified in the affidavit.
In other words, sir, if a minister or the cabinet decides that a certain document which has been subpoenaed by the court may be injurious to those things, the minister may sign an affidavit, give it to the judge, explain his reasons, and the judge could, and most often does, concur and keep the document secret.
Incidentally, the debate in 1970 centred on this business of federal-provincial relations. Why should the federal government have any secrets about its relationships with the provinces? That was the only thing that seemed to offend our learned friends who participated in the debate at that time. In any case, because of the very unique position the Federal Court has in a democracy, or in a system such as ours, it can make that decision, and the only other person who would know about the contents of that document would, of course, be the judge.
Subsection (2), which was inserted in 1970 and which became law in 1972, states:
(2) When a minister of the Crown certifies to any court by affidavit that the production or discovery of a document or its contents would be injurious to international relations, national defence or security, or to federal-provincial relations, or that it would disclose a confidence of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada, discovery and production shall be refused without any examination of the document by the court.
Subsection (2) clearly introduces an entirely new dimension to the relationship between the judiciary and the government, and the judiciary and Parliament. 1 suggest that this new dimension is extremely and exceedingly dangerous, particularly since it is so open to abuse. It raises suspicion. Too much secrecy always raises suspicion and gives an indication that someone has something to hide. Indeed, I would like to think that we are coming to the end of the era in which the order of the day was secrecy and in which there was a paranoia
Federal Court Act
throughout the land about subversive elements threatening the orderly enforcement of law and the integrity of our system from within.
There is no doubt that much of the feeling of alienation from the truth is now finding expression in terms of separatism and dissent and that events around us in the last few days and which will culminate today in fact are very much attributable to the stubborn, aloof and secretive attitude of the Trudeau government since 1968. In the last few days we have been reaping the harvest of the seeds of suspicion which were sown in the era of the 1970s.
Even though members of the law profession did not speak out when this bill was first introduced and when changes were made and subsection (2) was added to the Federal Court Act, others have. 1 am drawing on a reference made by one Justice Deschenes who, as hon. members know, heard the case of the two young ladies who were wrongfully dismissed from the Olympic committee during the 1976 Olympics in Quebec. Judge Deschenes had this to say:
Indeed, it is one of the strange contradictions of the Federal Court Act that an act which generally gives the courts greater authority over the excutivc branch of government, should at the time show a lack of faith in the integrity of the courts to responsibly adjudicate in all cases on claims of Crown privilege and protect the genuine security interests of the state.
Justice McDonald, who is chief commissioner of the McDonald commission, had similar reservations about section 41(2). He questioned how he could discharge his responsibility if ministers of the Crown forbade him access to important documents which were obviously required by the commission before it could make a judgment with respect to the relationship between the individual, our society and the law.
Let me give a couple of examples of how individuals can be affected by this particular section of the Federal Court Act. 1 would like to refer briefly to the case of one Walter Rudnicki. This is not the first time that I have mentioned Mr. Rudnicki in the House or the problems he experienced in connection with his dealings with cabinet and which ended up in court. Again it was a case of wrongful dismissal. Mr. Rudnicki eventually won the court action, but the reasons for his dismissal were never made public. I suppose only Mr. Rudnicki, a couple of my colleagues and a number of ministers of the Crown and 1 know why Mr. Rudnicki was actually fired from the public service. Mr. Rudnicki's name was included on a list of names which was termed "extra-parliamentary opposition". It was a list of people who were considered subversive to our system and who were plotting to replace our represent political system with radical alternatives.
Anyone who knows Mr. Rudnicki or any of the other 21 names mentioned on that list would know that it was just so much nonsense. In fact, Mr. Rudnicki may have been in extra-parliamentary opposition to the then Liberal government, but he was certainly a visible supporter of Her Majesty's loyal opposition. In no way was Mr. Rudnicki planning to replace this system of government with any radical alternatives. Nevertheless, his name was included in this list which a

May 20, 1980
Federal Court Act
former solicitor general chose to circulate to senior public servants and his colleagues as a means of warning them about Mr. Rudnicki and his tendencies.
As a result Mr. Rudnicki was fired. How was he to clear his name? I have attempted in this House to clear his name and to help him with his plight. I would like to read a short reference to what happened in the House on May 24, 1977. I said:
-during the question period, the term "extra-parliamentary opposition" was first introduced into the records of the House. The then minister of state for urban affairs was questioned about the existence of a blacklist connected with this term. He asserted that the blacklist charge was very serious. Fortunately though, he added, it was without foundation.
On January 24, 1977, I questioned the Prime Minister... about the list. He responded by saying, "I have not the slightest idea what the hon. member is talking about". The very next day the Minister of Transport. .. said he had never heard or seen such a list. The President of the Privy Council... also pleaded total ignorance. On January 26 the Solicitor General . .. said no such thing existed, nor did it ever exist.
The reason I had asked all these people in succession was because the bottom of the list had indicated that they were the people who were receiving the list when it was first circulated. So all these people knew and, of course, the House knows as well, that the list did exist, that is was not only circulated to those ministers and the Prime Minister and discussed in the cabinet committee on security and intelligence, but that there were literally dozens of lists like it which were not only circulated within the cabinet but within certain departments among senior public servants and which were also given to foreign countries to add to their records on subversives.
How was Rudnicki ever to clear his name? First he would need the money for a lawyer who would then be required to subpoena certain documents and ministers of the Crown to appear in court to show indeed that there was such a list, that his name was on it and that that was the reason for which he was dismissed from the public service.
Of course, there are literally hundreds of such cases to which one could make direct reference. Another such case is that of one Ursula Najder. She fell victim to another secret practice which relates to security clearance of persons who apply for positions in the public service and in some cases in the private sector as well. 1 would like to quote from a page of a secret document which deals with the practice of security clearance:
Authorities concerned should be aware of the fact that there are certain categories of persons which arc not normally clearable, at least beyond the level of CONFIDENTIAL, not because of doubts as to loyalty or reliability but because of circumstances such as:
1.1	close relatives living within the borders of such foreign nations as may
cause him to be subjected to intolerable pressures; or
1.2	recent residence (within the past ten years) in foreign countries where
no check of activities is possible.
In the case of Ursula Najder, she is a Canadian by birth, but her parents came to Canada from Poland. Ursula Najder still had an aunt in Poland which she had met, I believe, twice in her life. Because she had an aunt in a country in which Canada cannot carry out normal security checks, Ursula Najder, and probably 25 per cent of all Canadians who came from parts of the world where security checks cannot be made,
was denied a job with the public service, to which she was entitled.
It goes further because one can be with a firm that has a contract with the federal government having to do with procurement of armaments or whatever. In other words, where a certian degree of secrecy and confidentiality is required. Ursula Najder could not get a job at that private company because the same kind of security clearance applied. How is she to fight for her rights if an effort that she might make before a court could be frustrated simply by the fact that a minister's statement says that a document which she might need to state her case is not available to the court because it is injurious to cabinet secrecy, federal-provincial relations or whatever?
At the outset 1 said that there appears to be a general inclination to move toward greater freedom of information. It is clear to me that it is essential and necessary-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased indeed to have the opportunity of speaking on Bill C-202, to amend the Federal Court Act. I think the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has brought forth a very timely bill before this House of Commons, one whose substance has been talked about for a considerable period of time. I am disappointed that he could suggest, maybe inadvertently or otherwise, that there are too many lawyers in the House of Commons and none saw fit to bring this bill forward. However, I might point out to him that many lawyers have been working on this problem for a considerable length of time, and as the hon. member knows, because he has looked at the statutes and the cases, there is a great deal of case law on it at the present time which supports something that goes a great deal further than what he has mentioned here in the House today.
This bill proposes to amend section 41 of the Federal Court Act so as to leave with the courts exclusive authority to decide whether documents ought or ought not to be disclosed in the course of litigation when objection is taken to their production on grounds of protecting the interests of the state.
The present provisions of section 41 formed part of the original Federal Court Act enacted in 1970 and were intended to reflect the results of judicial decisions up to that time on so-called Crown privilege. Those decisions made it clear that the judiciary were to be the final arbiters of the public interests involved: that is to say, the courts were able to look at the documents objected to and determine whether the public interest favouring the proper administration of justice on behalf of the litigants was or was not outweighed by the public interest in favour of the interest of the state. This formulation of principle was translated into section 41(1) of the Federal Court Act, as the hon. member knows.
May 20, 1980

However, those cases also indicated that this general principle perhaps had no application to extremely important state documents dealing with such matters as international relations, matters of defence, cabinet matters and communications between ministers and senior civil servants. The absolute exclusion of documents falling into any of these classes of highly sensitive state information was provided for by section 42(2) of the Federal Court Act, which was read into the record by the hon. member.
In the past few years, subsection (2) in particular has received a good deal of criticism, and rightfully so. One criticism is that the courts are well equipped to balance the public interests at stake and have a traditional role in doing so. The mere fact that the Crown may, on occasion, consider that some documents are more sensitive does not mean that this role should be removed entirely from the judiciary. Adding substance to this criticism is the fact that under these provisions a minister of the Crown is able to deny the courts any authority to look at the documents in issue.
These criticisms have been given additional weight by virtue of recent decisions of the highest courts of the land in Great Britain, the United States and Australia, to name only three countries, which have confirmed that the courts in all cases- and 1 am sure the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn) will be glad to hear this-have the power to examine the documents objected to and to balance the public interests at stake.
At the same time, a good deal of thought and attention was being paid to proposals for freedom of information legislation. While the importance of disclosure is far more important in the case of Crown privilege, access to government documents by members of the public is essential to both. It is not surprising to find that the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and other Statutory Instruments, of which I was a member along with the hon. member for Saskatoon West, agreed unanimously in its report in June, 1978, that:
Your committee finds that section 41(2) (of the Federal Court Act) is inconsistent with the principles to be established in a freedom of information statute and therefore recommends that it be repealed.
This more comprehensive approach to dealing with section 41 of the Federal Court Act seems to me to be the wiser course to take and is the one that the government has proposed. In the Speech from the Throne it is stated:
Members of Parliament, whatever their party, agree on the need to guarantee to Canadians greater access to information of concern to them. Freedom of information legislation will be introduced to provide wide access to government documents. The right accorded to ministers to withold government documents from courts of law under section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act will be repealed.
I note that in the statement in the Speech from the Throne it may be considered an inconsistency that it refers only to documents, whereas the present section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act refers to documents or a document or its contents. This may be semantics to some extent, but on the other hand it could be rather important.
I note once again that the member from Saskatoon West referred to a question on section 41 in the House of Commons
Federal Court Act
recently. I do not know whether he was referring to that specific aspect of it, but it could be important. Also when one takes a look at section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act, which refers to discovery and production, there is quite a difference between discovery and production in the context of a document or its contents. I merely point that out for hon. members.
As for the substance of the bill now before the House, I believe there are a number of matters which bear comment. First of all, the bill confines itself to disclosure of documents. However, Crown privilege extends to all forms of evidence and, consequently, the bill would retain a limitation already present in section 41. It is for that reason that the proposals in the freedom of information bill of the last Parliament, of which the hon. member who presented this bill was a member, replaced the word "document" with the more general term "information". I think this may be considered very important, particularly since, as I mentioned before, section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act refers to a document or its contents, and now we are talking about a document or information. So this too is an important aspect to be considered.
Secondly, the bill applies only to court actions. The production and discovery of information is, of course, not confined to courts, and in fact there are decisions on the basis of the word "tribunal", which is the term in the French version of section 41, which have held that this provision applies to administrative bodies acting quasi-judicially in the exercise of their power to compel the production of documents. It is because of the doubts and confusion that surround the reference to "court" alone in section 41 that the proposals in the freedom of information bill would use wider language encompassing not only courts but as well all bodies having the power to compel the production of the sort of government information that may require protection from disclosure on the ground of state interest.
Thirdly, the bill would retain the classes of documents listed in section 41(2), which the hon. member and I have read into the record. These have raised so many objections in the past that they must be addressed at this time. It is true that the bill would permit a court to examine the documents in question, but by distinguishing between these special classes of documents and any other public interest of the state, the bill may well be perceived as attempting to make a basic qualitative distinction between the two and unnecessarily favouring documents in the list of classes. It certainly might be suggested that such a distinction would create non-confidence in the courts to recognize the special importance of certain kinds of government information. If the courts of other common law jurisdictions have been able to handle these classes of information without the benefit of special legislation in their favour, it may be asked whether this aspect of the bill is really necessary.
Fourthly, some very real procedural difficulties are ignored in the bill. If, as the case law on section 41 now holds, "court" includes tribunals exercising quasi-judicial powers, it may be asked whether the members of such bodies should have the

May 20, 1980
Federal Court Act
same powers as the courts to examine such potentially sensitive and injurious information. The same question may be asked about the courts themselves; should a justice of the peace or provincial court judge or magistrate be entrusted with the same powers here as, for example, a superior court judge?
We do not have time to go into all the details and ramifications of that, but it is a serious and important question to be asked, whether in a very simple case before a minor court official such as a justice of the peace or junior magistrate, one should be bringing forth a matter so important that in the past it was considered a matter to be addressed to a supreme court judge.
Whatever the answers to these questions may be, there is also the problem of what procedure ought to be followed if, for example, the trial court or the tribunal orders production. Should not the Crown have the right to pursue the matter on appeal before the document has been disclosed to the parties and to the public thereby nullifying the practical effects of an appeal and, more important, making public some possibly very sensitive information? The bill says nothing about this critical procedural issue.
I would suggest to the hon. member that he might look at this when he is doing further research.
Fifthly, clause 41(1) of the bill appears to be an attempt to codify the rules of disclosure and discovery of documents. It has no equivalent in the present provisions of the act, and for good reason. Such a provision is usually to be found in rules of court where it is subject to a variety of exceptions and to the flexibility that matters of procedure like this must retain. In statutory form and subject only to the exception in subclause (2), this discovery and production provision may well be far more absolute than anyone, including the sponsor of the bill, would wish. For example, is subclause (1) subject to solicitor-client privilege? This is a very important matter.
When we talk about privilege, I note that the province of Newfoundland recognizes the right of religious advisers as well as the question of solicitor-client privilege between a solicitor and client. Quebec gives more extensive protection. Indeed, the code of civil procedure of Quebec grants privilege to clergymen, lawyers, notaries, physicians and dentists. I do not know how far we go in this, but so far Quebec is the only province to go quite that far. Is it subject to other privileges and exceptions in this area? Is it subject to the non-disclosure provisions in other statutes?
It seems to me that this subclause is both dangerous and unwarranted. It adds little or nothing to what the bill seeks to achieve. And it is therefore understandable why no such provision was included either in the present section 41 or in the redrafted version proposed in the freedom of information bill, Bill C-15, in the last Parliament.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest, first, that there are specific aspects of the bill that require a good deal of thought, and, second, that the very limited objectives of the bill have been overtaken by events that require section 41 to be examined in the context of access to government information
in general. It was no doubt in recognition of this that the previous government proposed the changes to section 41 which were contained in their freedom of information bill introduced during the last session which certainly went further than the changes proposed in this bill.
On page 31 of Bill C-15 presented by the last government, an act to extend the present laws of Canada that provide access to information under the control of the Government of Canada and to amend the Canada Evidence Act, the Federal Court Act and the Statutory Instruments Act, clause 70 reads:
Section 41 of the Federal Court Act is repealed.
I note the hon. member does not go that far. This indicates to me he intends to retain section 41(1) and only remove subsection (2) of section 41 of the Federal Court Act. When we look at it from that point of view, it seems that he is not following the present law as enunciated by most of the courts of jurisdiction in the number of countries that I mentioned, and others as well. It certainly does not follow the suggestions made in the Speech from the Throne that I mentioned previously. 1 am sure it does not comply with the suggestions made by the hon. member's own party.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to say a few words on this bill. At first glance this is a bill which is designed to increase the access of citizens to government information. It is a freedom of information bill, one of a long and honourable series of attempts in this House to open the doors to government files, to shed some light on the information at the government's disposal.
Seen simply as a freedom of information bill, I must say that 1 and my party are sympathetic to the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) and his intentions. If he is joining the long fight to create a right of access for the citizens who pay for government information in the first place, then I congratulate him for joining a most worthy cause, and l welcome him to make further efforts in this direction.
I am happy to point out that the first freedom of information legislation to be introduced to this House was also a private member's bill, brought forward by the New Democratic Party member Barry Mather from New Westminster, in 1965. The torch was thrown to the former hon. member for Peace River, Mr. Baldwin, who kept the issue alive through many years, culminating finally in the introduction of a government bill last year, Bill C-15.
I wish to remind this House that the NDP supported Bill C-15 last November 29, and agreed to a speedy second reading so that the bill could quickly go to committee for further study. We had many reservations about the details of the bill. The exemptions were drafted too broadly, for example, and needed to be tightened up. My colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), said that you could drive a truck through some of the loopholes in Bill C-15 and that this must be rectified. But we supported the principle nevertheless, and that is why I congratulate the hon. member for his sentiments in introducing a bill along the same general lines.
May 20, 1980

1 well remember that night in the House of Commons during the first session of Parliament that I had the privilege to attend. For me it was one of the highlights of that session. It was an exciting moment when the then hon. member for Peace River demonstrated to me and a lot of other new members the force of a member who has an idea and the willingness and perseverance to follow it through. On that occasion he spoke eloquently about his fight in this matter and stated that that probably was the last piece of legislation with which he would be involved. That, historically, proved correct as the House came down within a matter of days.
We believe that any move which will foster the exposure of the truth in society is beneficial. Whether we are are defending a free press, free speech, or free access to government information, we are defending the cause of truth. In this particular area, my experience living and working in many other countries makes me realize that this is one of the key issues involving the whole question of a person's rights. Truth, simply put, makes people free, if it is truth total and whole. However, when legislation, whatever kind it may be, is used in such a way to hold back total and complete truth, instead of making people free what happens is that they become slaves, and the power that is given over the those in charge takes away the freedom of individuals. 1 have seen that happen.
The legislation proposed in Bill C-202 before the House this afternoon is not exactly what we had in mind for freedom of information legislation for this country. The bill attempts to do through the back door what Bill C-15 would have done through the front door. It is half a step toward freedom of information. Actually it is less than half a step. And for that reason 1 have my doubts about the bill. We believe that the issues should be faced squarely in a separate freedom of information act, not in an amendment to the Federal Court Act. We expect the new government to honour its commitment given in the throne speech to introduce a freedom of information bill in this session. 1 am surprised that it has not been introduced already. I do expect it soon. At that time we can get down to the serious business of working out the precise wording of the new law. I am sure that all parties welcome the chance to pick up where we left off last fall.
[DOT] <1740)
Part of the new legislation will have to deal with section 41 of the Federal Court Act. There is no doubt that section 41 needs to be changed. At present it is an unwarranted hindrance to the rights of litigators. It is an affront to our belief that citizens should have access to government information with only the narrowest of exceptions. But to amend section 41 right now in the absence of a comprehensive freedom of information act makes no sense. It is not just litigators who should have a right to access but all citizens regardless of the purpose for which they would use the information sought. An amendment such as the one proposed in the bill before us is more likely to hinder full freedom of information than to help it, and for that reason I doubt the wisdom of introducing it at this time.
Federal Court Act
Bill C-15 of last year simply repealed section 41 of the Federal Court Act. No section was to be substituted, it was just scratched. I like this approach. Once the rights of all citizens are decided in a freedom of information act, then the rights of litigators before the Federal Court fall into place. This is fair and just, and I support the approach taken by Bill C-15 in this regard.

speechtext: Would the hon. member accept a question? He states quite categorically that in Bill C-15 which was being presented by the former government, section 41 of the Federal Court Act would be repealed. But has he looked at the rest of the bill to determine whether some aspects of that section creep back into the bill through the back door?

I believe that is possible and that the section will creep back in. But I think a serious study of the bill in committee by all parties with an open mind would ensure proper handling of that kind of thing. The hon. member's former colleague from Peace River, Mr. Baldwin, proposed a slightly different approach to section 41. But he, too, would have made a freedom of information act paramount.
The hon. member's proposal would put the courts in a difficult spot. In every case they would become embroiled in substantive questions of freedom of information law and procedure. This would slow down the court process and confuse the issues. We say that the question of what government documents a citizen should get is a prior question which should be decided by an over-all freedom of information act, not on an individual basis in the course of each trial.
In some other respects, I disagree with the approach taken by the bill before the House. For example, in subclause (2)(b) the words "national security" appear. What is meant by national security? I could speak at length about that particular phraseology as it is understood in some other countries where everything that happens finally comes under some form of national security, and human rights of all kinds disappear as this notion of national security is interpreted by those in charge of law making and the courts. I am sure these words will be used as a pretext by government and the courts for withholding all sorts of information which should rightly be in the public domain.
The danger of using words such as "national security" has been clearly set out by Professor Murray Rankin in a paper entitled "Freedom of Information in Canada; Will The Doors Stay Shut?" I agree that the words "national security" should not be used; a tighter definition must be presented which will safeguard the public's right to know. That is what I and my party stand for-a complete freedom of information act which will guarantee truth for all at all times.

Mr. Speaker, my intervention in this debate will be brief. I listened with interest to participation by the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), and to the response of the parliamentary secretary which, frankly, raised some

Federal Court Act
question in my mind with respect to the government's intention with regard to its commitments made in the Speech from the Throne.
I commend the hon. member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ogle), that great centre of all good, truth and justice, for his comments and his support for the principle of freedom of information. The hon. member referred to the fact that he had lived in a number of countries around the world where information of any sort is hard to come by. He has experienced at first hand some political regimes in which there is denial of the right of individual citizens to obtain information from government. I am sure it was by inadvertance that the hon. member omitted to tell us that he now resides in the province of Saskatchewan. We know the position which has been taken by the provincial government of that province when requested to bring in freedom of information legislation. They unanimously refused to follow that course of action. So I am sure he and I will work together in Saskatoon to prevail upon the provincial government, the NDP government there, to bring in freedom of information legislation, because they are among the last hold-outs in terms of such legislation in Canada. The policy of the government there is against the concept of freedom of information. So 1 look forward to joining arms with the hon. member and facing the challenge of bringing truth, justice and right thinking to the government of Saskatchewan in this area. 1 know I will have his unqualified support.
My reason for entering this debate, though, is the response given by the parliamentary secretary with respect to the particular initiative upon which I commend my hon. friend. The fact is, he has been vigilant and insistent in his support of the principle of freedom of information. He has been trying to bring about amendments to the Federal Court Act, to section 41 and to section 41(2) in particular.
When we recall the wording of the Speech from the Throne we are reminded there was a paragraph in part four about strengthening national institutions. I want to quote from that particular section of the speech in which the government, through the Governor General, stated that "the right accorded to ministers to withhold government documents from courts of law under section 41(2) of the Federal Court Act will be removed." As I understand it, that was an unqualified commitment on the part of the government. However, 1 got the impression from the parliamentary secretary that a different approach might now be taken and that perhaps a reversal of that position might be expected-that rather than removing this right from ministers the government is considering amending the provisions of section 41(2) because of considerations which have occurred to them subsequent to the preparation of the Speech from the Throne and that the intent of the commitment might not be followed through.
I hope that that is not going to be the case, and I am very interested in finding out whether we now have a departure, so soon after April 14, 1980, by this government, having regard to the fact that in the House of Commons in the course of
question periods the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) and, in fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself at other times, have indicated that freedom of information is the prime commitment of this government and that the operation of government is going to proceed, until that legislation is brought forward, on the basis that the principles of freedom of information will be observed. I take it impliedly that the commitment with respect to the right of ministers to withhold documents from courts will also be observed by this government.
I have raised in the House of Commons the case in which, shortly after the new government was sworn in, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) invoked the provisions of this particular section to withhold documents from an inquiry in the Federal Court before Mr. Justice Gibson with respect to the policies and practices of the Canadian Dairy Commission.
What concerns me about this-and 1 take no issue with the idea that freedom of information and the provisions of the Federal Court Act are necessarily associated-and what I would like to find out today, is whether or not the government is in fact retreating from the commitment made in the Speech from the Throne because, if that is the case, we are going to have a battle royal in this House on the basis of one of the greatest reversals in policy on a matter of fundamental importance, that we have seen for many years in the House of Commons. I think it is unacceptable for the government now to try to change its position.

One of the things about which we must be very cautious-and I have to caution the government on this-is that the government must be much more sensitive in the future than it has in the past because many of the problems that Canada and Canadians have had over the past several years have come as a result of an insensitive administration. You cannot ride roughshod over a people or a region, and 1 hope that in any talks that will be held in the future, consideration will be given to the manner in which our government will be operated on the three levels of administration.
Today the debate has to do primarily with the municipal level or the third level of administration. We must realize that this level of government is much closer to the people than either of the other two levels, and therefore I feel that consideration must be given to that body of people which operates within that sphere. 1 do not think the federal government has been particularly careful so far as the municipal level is concerned and so far as taxation is concerned. 1 recognize that the bill has to do with government institutions and, as 1 mentioned earlier, so far as jails are concerned those institutions take away a great deal of the tax base on which rural municipalities rely.
As I said earlier, prior to the private members' hour, taking that base away from the municipal bodies means that they have less money on which to function when the federal government does not pay its share. I also feel at this time that we should give some consideration to Crown corporations, and I would like to take a few moments to deal with one of those Crown corporations, namely, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. 1 have a notice of motion before the House. I do not know whether or not there will be an opportunity to debate it, but I would like to bring it to the attention of the House at this time. It reads as follows:
That in the opinion of this House the government should consider the advisability of increasing the grants made to municipalities in lieu of property taxes for the use of property by Crown corporations and agencies so that these grants equal the sums paid by private organizations.
We have a case in my constituency where the CBC is in competition with two other private bodies. The private bodies have to pay the assessed rate of tax and, at the same time, in paying their taxes, they subsidize their competitor, which in this case is the CBC. Also, the CBC does not have to pay its fair share of the taxes, or an equal portion of the taxes that these other private companies have to pay. In this case, according to the assessment, the CBC should be paying $4,480.53. What are they paying? They are paying $617.92. To me, that is not justice. I took this case up with the CBC, and on November 2 of last year 1 sent a memo to the corporation. This is the question 1 asked:
Has the CBC legislated authority to establish its corporate policy, or is it obliged to abide by rates of other radio stations in the same locality?
This is the answer I got:
In response to your memorandum of November 2, I am pleased to forward to you, the following information.
The CBC, a Crown corporation, is exempt from municipal property taxation. In 1951, the federal government decided to compensate municipalities, by way of grants in lieu of taxes, for the fact that federal government properties were exempt from taxation, but the resulting Municipal Grants Act (1951) excluded the CBC.
In 1957, the board of directors of the CBC adopted a resolution to pay grants in lieu of taxes in a manner similar to the terms of the Municipal Grants Act.
There is legislated authority to exempt the CBC from paying anything in lieu of taxes, but CBC policy does permit a grant on the assessed value of land, buildings and heating plant only. In accordance with the terms of the act, movable property such as the tower and equipment would be excluded from the assessment.
There does not seem to be much that can be done in this situation, but I am enclosing a number of newspaper clippings from the Library of Parliament to give you some background on how similar problems have been confronted in other areas.
This communication was signed by Kay Marshall.
In these clippings from the Library of Parliament I find that this problem goes back to 1974. After six years of debate, confrontation and requests, surely the government should be able to deal with this situation and come to grips with it. I say the government must be sensitive in this particular area. I believe this is one of the main ones, primarily because of the fact that rural municipalities are deprived of the taxation base that is theirs and should be theirs, one which I think they are justified in expecting to receive, and are not. In whatever talks, debates or discussions take place in the future, I would hope that consideration is given to this so that these municipalities can have their fair share.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose all of us are debating this bill on an evening when the attention of the Canadian public is directed elsewhere to momentous events which are occurring in one of our provinces. I think all of us who watched the results coming in on television were gratified with the results thus far in the referendum in the province of Quebec.
There seems to be a large commitment on behalf of the people of Quebec, at least at this stage of the proceedings, to the idea of federalism. Perhaps it is important that there be that kind of commitment. I suppose it would not be found out of favour with Mr. Speaker if I said, at this point in time, that this large commitment by the province of Quebec to federalism has its counter engagement with respect to a great commitment that is expected of the rest of Canada regarding renewed federalism. I suspect when the results come in, if the present trend holds, that the people of Quebec will be looking to the rest of Canada to ask them about what is their commitment to renewed federalism. They will be looking to the premiers who have spoken so importantly about renewed federalism. They will be looking to the members of this House of Commons who have spoken in the course of debate and talked about the importance of renewed federalism.
We must make no mistake; the results tonight are important to this country. While they are important to the country, there is a much greater period of time ahead of us in terms of perhaps constitutional change and certainly of renewed federalism that will be of far more significance in the long run to the future of Canada, and that is the relationship among the governments of this country in the years to come.
When I rise to speak for the first time this session in debate on a major bill in the House of Commons, though 1 have been on my feet from time to time, 1 must take advantage of this opportunity to congratulate Madam Speaker on her ascension to the chair. I have enjoyed working with her in the course of my duties as House leader. Also I have enjoyed working with you, Mr. Speaker. We share neighbouring ridings; we share many of the same problems. I hope Mr. Speaker will forgive me if, in the course of the debate, 1 quote some of your words to the government with respect to the issue before us and perhaps one other issue with which we might be dealing later on in the evening.
I am very pleased to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) in the House tonight. It is a refreshing change to have a minister of the Crown staying in the House while his or her bill is being debated. It may be because the minister got his early training in municipal politics, which is a very demanding field. 1 do not agree very often with the things the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) does, but I think it is important that the Minister of Public Works has some municipal background.
While this bill certainly affects municipalities all across the country, it has a profound effect upon one municipality directly in this area. It is a municipality which 1 do not represent. In part it is represented by the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), in part by the hon. member for Ottawa West
Grants to Municipalities
(Mr. Francis), and in part by the hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), but it has a spin-off effect on the municipalities which I represent. So, it is important in that area.
I think it is rather appropriate that a former municipal politician who came to his senses and came into the relatively easy field of federal politics is piloting this bill through the House of Commons. I say that in the best of faith. I have never served in the municipal field. There are some members in this House who will say, "Thank God for that". But I served in another way when I had the privilege of practising law in this area. I acted for a large number of municipalities locally. I saw the pressures to which municipal politicians are subject, very direct pressures with respect to a minimum amount of financial clout in terms of the ability to raise the money themselves, a great dependence on the provinces, tremendous problems which have to be solved, and a very difficult job of priorizing.
This bill which will provide additional moneys to 2,000 municipalities in this country will be extremely helpful. As I say, I think this bill is important, and I think it is quite fitting that this bill should be introduced by a politician who came into public life via the municipal field.
1 do not want to be partisan, because people know I am not partisan by nature. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier is sitting across the way. He knows me not to be a partisan person. But I must remind the House of some of the history of this legislation. When the present Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Chretien) was minister of finance back in the Thirtieth Parliament, a similar bill to this one was numbered C-46. That is a long way down the pecking order. It is getting close to the numbering system we use for private bills in this House. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, the hon. member for Ottawa West, the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick), the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, as he then was, or the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton, as he now is, together asked question after question in the House as to when they would bring forward this legislation. Nothing happened, except that the bill was introduced. I do not believe it was even debated in the Thirtieth Parliament.
Then came the Clark government. The Clark government had as its minister of finance a man of extreme kindness, understanding and concern, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). He was prevailed upon with respect to the importance of this kind of legislation for local government, the kind of government which I described as having a great part of the burden to bear in terms of the difficult job of priorizing- priorizing the use of funds in an area of diminishing returns. As a result of the priority he put on it, lo and behold, in the Thirty-first Parliament with the Clark government that bill ascended in the pecking order and became Bill C-3.
I want to thank the hon. member for St. John's West for giving it that priority, because he gave some leadership in respect of the problem of the financing of municipalities. He gave some leadership to the extent that this reincarnated

government we have before us in this Thirty-second Parliament has numbered this bill C-4. That is a great improvement. It is an improvement of ten times, from C-46 to C-4. We are now debatin^This bill and hopefully we will see it through the second reading stage in a relatively short period so that it can be studied by the committee and eventually passed.
This is the kind of legislation which recognizes the importance of local government, and recognizes its financial inadequacies from time to time having regard to the mandate it has. Unfortunately this delay from the Thirtieth Parliament to today has caused Canadian municipalities to iose the benefit of this legislation, from the time it was first mooted as important and accepted as a commitment by the Liberal government which preceded this one. I say this to you in historical terms. It is an important piece of legislation and we are happy to see it here.
1 do not have to stress to the Minister of Public Works the tremendous costs involved in providing services to government buildings, and providing services generally in communities, especially a community like the one I represent, and there are others across the country in equal shape.
When you look at the scope of the bill you see that it updates the Municipal Grants Act under which the government now pays, I think, $148 million each year in grants on federal properties located in about 2,000 municipalities. These grants will be increased by $25.5 million during a four-year phase period starting this year. The coverage is extensive. It covers such things, as far as we are concerned, as Parliament Hill, as the National Library and Archives, the National Arts Centre, the National Gallery, and the National Museum, all of which are in Ottawa. It covers a whole host of defence and other installations all across this country, from Greenwood and Shearwater on the one end and Victoria on the other end of Canada. This is truly a good piece of legislation.
1 am a little bit worried about the exclusions in the bill. 1 say to the minister, with respect, that I am concerned about the exclusions, and the arguments put forward for excluding such things as parklands, Indian reserves, and what he described as structures, and concerned to the extent that they are excluded from this bill on the basis set forth by that magnificent and generous former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West.
The grounds were, of course, that they were excluded because of the nature of the items, and because the local cost of providing services is minimal. However, to the extent that services are provided by local municipalities to these kind of installations, even those that may be described as minimal, there is a withdrawal of the ability of the federal government to contribute to the cost of local government.
1 feel that while we can regard this bill as the second word, the first word having occurred some 22 years ago when the first bill came forward, I do not think we can say we have reached the end of the road in terms of the generosity of the federal government. We should regard this bill as the second word in respect of municipal grants legislation, but we anticipate as we go ahead that we will hear the third word, which
will involve greater coverage of these structures; jetties, canal locks, aircraft runways, and a number of other things which do impact upon the finances that a municipality has to carry out its mandate.
There are some who say the national capital is a very fortunate area, and 1 think it is really quite a fortunate part of Canada. Those of us who live in it are grateful, quite frankly, for the fact that it is such a fortunate part of Canada. This is a unique city. The city of Ottawa, the national capital area generally, is unique because it is the national capital. As a national capital it has to exhibit some of the nation. The nation is not all government; there is industrial and business development that ought to be encouraged in the national capital area.
It is a fact, and I think you know this, Mr. Speaker, that this bill will go a long way to ameliorate the differential in municipal tax rates which has been in place for some period of time. There has been some difficulty in attracting to Ottawa some of the diversification potential that must occur if this city is not only to be a microcosm of Canada, as Mr. Danson once described it, or what it should be on the one hand, and an area that provides a variety of employment for young people, on the other hand.
As a result of this differential that has existed, there has been a great tendency to rely on the federal government as the sole employer. I know there is high technology industry developing here. This bill will make it attractive to other people to come here because the tax differential will be right and we can do some work on direct air connection to Chicago, New York and Boston, and a few other things such as that which would not cost the federal government any money. We can perhaps consider at some stage upgrading the Ottawa International Airport. The Minister of Public Works might consider that as being helpful in enhancing this place as the national capital.
By and large this bill in terms of its area of potential is important for local government. Some people in local government say it is not enough. I would be inclined to agree that anyone who represents an area that is getting the benefit would say it is not enough, but it is a good beginning. I think the minister should be commended for bringing it forward once again and for giving it such high priority. It is something that the commercial and industrial corporations in the Ottawa area, the Board of Trade, the Nepean Chamber of Commerce, the Regional Municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and others have been seeking for some considerable time.
There is a hang-up about this legislation, and that is the term "business tax". Members have spoken about it, and I think we are hung up on the language. If it were called anything else but business tax this government and the experts of the Department of Finance, some of whom are here tonight, might be able to take a different view of it. I would hope they could, and I am looking to them and entreating them to take a different view.
There are services that are provided by a municipality which are not covered by the general tax rate levied against the property. There are, in fact, even departments of government
May 20, 1980

which, under some examination, might be deemed to be carrying on a business. Certainly Crown corporations do, and there is a differential in regard to businesses being carried on by the government through Crown corporations and those in the private sector, as some hon. members have shown.
If the federal government is going to carry its full load, then we have to look at the operations of departments. If there is a hang-up in government in considering a contribution toward what would otherwise be called "business tax", in order that it is carrying its full load in all municipalities, not just this one, then let us take a look at some other semantic. Let us not be hung up on that phrase "business tax", so that we will be considering increasing the contribution to the municipal good will as a result of the service which must be supplied to government and which government should pay for just like everyone else.
I hope that at the committee stage of this bill the municipal leaders and organizations in Canada will be called by the committee to come and review the bill. I do not think that consideration should be long, but 1 do think that Parliament should have the best advice it can get from the people who deal with the municipal problems, to see whether any of the matters which were discussed and which were important at an earlier stage have changed and whether there are not new considerations involved of a different nature. In this way the government will know the general feeling with respect to this bill, and when it contemplates further legislation, that further legislation will be as up to date as the public purse will allow, and the municipalities will have the benefit of the government carrying the freight.
I would like to talk for a moment about the good fortune which 1 feel and which every person who lives in this area feels because of the presence of the federal government in the area. Not only is it a place for employment, but the federal government, through the auspices and good will of the people of Canada, has contributed a great deal to the development of this city and the area.
1 have never met a group which has come to visit Ottawa and the Parliament Buildings to which 1 have not expressed my thanks as a resident of the area. These are the people who foot the bill to a great extent for what we as residents have here and what members of Parliament who come to this city enjoy. It is a city of amenities, the likes of which are provided nowhere else. On either side of the Ottawa River these amenities can be found. There is the tremendous parkway system on the Ontario side and the magnificent Gatineau Park on the Quebec side. These developments did not come out of the federal government alone. They were contributed to by the taxpayers from across this country.
The Minister of Public Works has a tremendous responsibility, as the minister who answers in this House of Commons for the National Capital Commission, to continue the work which was begun with the planning of Mr. Greber. Prime ministers have also shown an interest in the national capital area. The
Grants to Municipalities
prime minister who took perhaps the greatest interest at the outset was Mackenzie King. That interest has been taken up by successive prime ministers who were interested in the development of a national capital. The Right Hon. John Diefenbaker during his government in 1958 brought in the National Capital Commission Act. This is a fact which none of us should forget. It declared the area on both sides of the Ottawa River to be the national capital region.
The British North America Act was not changed, the area was simply declared as the national capital region. As a result of this declaration the government was in a position to make tremendous contributions to the development of a system of amenities on this and the other side of the river which all of us enjoy. I hope the Minister of Public Works will consider, in his capacity as chairman of the National Capital Commission, that while there seems to be fairly good co-operation between the local government and the federal government agencies at the staff level, somehow or other at the policy level the consultative atmosphere is not as good as it should be. I do not know where to assess the blame, nor do I think that it is the job of any of us to assess the blame, but it is a fact which exists.
It would be in the best interests of the federal government, of the local government, and in the best interests of planning, development, and the future of the national capital, if the minister gave earnest consideration to a proposal which was first put forward by a member from our side, Mrs. Jean Pigott, when she was the member for Ottawa-Carleton, with regard to membership on the National Capital Commission of the chairmen of the two regional municipalities on either side of the river. Whether we are talking about the development of a tax policy, a sharing policy, or whatever it is, those people from across this country who are commissioners would have the advice of those local people. I hope that this idea will be considered.
There is a tremendous regulatory process in this piece of legislation, as there is in every piece of legislation that seems to be brought forward by successive governments. I hope, as regulations are made, as new regulations are promulgated to replace those that are made, and as the process goes on, that before regulations take effect they will be published in The Canada Gazette in advance for the benefit of those groups, associations, municipal governments and others which will be affected.
However, well meaning public servants may be, however well meaning ministries or ministers may be, slips can happen and misjudgments can be made. It serves the process well if, before a regulation takes effect, the government will publish it well in advance. This would be very helpful in the development of the process. There are tremendous areas of land to be developed. The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier mentioned LeBreton Flats with regard to the development and what might be done with the funding that would be available to the local municipality. 1 have some views, as I am sure you do, Mr. Speaker, on LeBreton Flats with regard to the use of that land. There will be differences of opinion, both locally and federally.
