The hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier also mentioned the development of Fournier Park in Hull and the Woodroffe demonstration project in our own area. There have been great negotiations between the federal government and the local government on this project. The federal government was represented by CMHC. The matter now seems to be in trouble. There is even some talk that the land will go to a private developer. I hope that that is the last thing that will happen to that property. I hope that that property stays within the public domain. To repeat it so that the minister understands my view, I hope that that property stays within the public domain, unless there is no alternative to that development. There are residents living close to that development who are counting on the land use remaining the same in terms of the future. It is a very important piece of property.
Later on we will be considering the relocation legislation. The federal government should take a look at that piece of property at the corner of Woodroffe and Baseline in terms of a federal development on that land. 1 suggest to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey), who was in the House a moment ago, that I have always felt that that property would be a good spot for a new taxation data centre. Everyone knows that the present facility for Revenue Canada at Confederation Heights is overutilized. I knew that when I was minister, and we were considering a place to put that data centre. That property is one good place which ought to be considered. Such a commitment to that valuable piece of property would be in keeping with the whole development of that area, the western parkway, and a whole host of other areas. Incidentally, it would improve the assessment base in the local municipality.
There is no job more difficult than satisfying the conflicting demands of various organizations which are put upon the Minister of Public Works, particularly in an area which is perhaps over governed in terms of levels of government. 1 sympathize with the minister completely. The minister has taken some of the burden off the local government sector through this piece of legislation. I wish that this legislation could have been introduced earlier, but now that it is here in the House I think that it should be supported and that it should go very quickly to committee where it can be dealt with in detail.

Mr. Speaker, this is the first opportunity that 1 have had to participate in the deliberations of this House. 1 would like to preface my remarks by first congratulating Madam Speaker on her election as Speaker, and yourself and your other colleagues on your appointments.
Second, I would like to inform hon. gentlemen opposite who are displaying anxiety symptoms about post-referendum Canada that the administration and party with the courage and conviction to fight and win the referendum will display the intellect and sensitivity necessary for successful constitutional reform.
I am pleased at this time to rise in support of Bill C-4 because 1 endorse the principles which have shaped it, namely, the expansion of the numbers and types of federal properties which will generate grant revenue for municipalities, the redefinition of the granting formula to approximate more closely the revenues which would have been generated by taxes on those properties, the creation of guidelines for Crown corporations to make them more sensitive to the demands of their respective municipal environments, the transfer of authority for these aforementioned responsibilities to the Ministry of Public Works, the speedy implementation by the federal government of the majority of the proposed reforms withirbthe year and all of the reforms within four years, and most important, the funnelling of more money, approximately $25 million, to a level of government whose services to all its constituents, governmental, business and residential, are as important as they are costly.
My support is not unequivocal. There are reservations. The definition of grant revenue properties may have to be expanded further. Grant rates might have to be increased and the retention of the arbitration authority by the federal government should be reinvestigated, for I believe a party to a dispute should not be permitted ultimately to settle a dispute.
These are matters of substance or content which will be properly and thoroughly reviewed by the appropriate standing committee, and should not deter any member from supporting this bill this afternoon and evening.
In conclusion, this bill has been before the House on three separate occasions within a short span of one and one-half years. Anything that can be said about it has been said. Let us not delay any longer. It deserves the speedy and unanimous support of this House.

Mr. Speaker, 1 will be brief. First, 1 want to deal with the principle very quickly and, second, I want to deal with a couple of details contained within the bill.
I do not know why it is that we perpetuate a system that places the Crown in a different position from the public. I do not know why we have not adopted recommendations made years ago to allow for tax to be levied against buildings owned by the Crown, whether owned federally or provincially, and the tax therefore to be paid in the same way as all other taxes are paid. Also, a problem tends to arise in municipalities with regard to accurate assessment of Crown-owned buildings. There is also the power that is used by the government in this bill of setting out the exemptions on which it will not pay tax.
It is interesting that the government decides that, for whatever reason, it just simply will not pay a grant for certain kinds of structures. That, of course, makes me wonder what would happen if some private individual were to build a similar structure. The individual would be taxed and would have to pay the tax. I do not quite understand why the Crown takes a different position.
I can remember when Chief Justice McRuer studied the property tax system in the province of Ontario and made many
May 20, 1980

recommendations, many of which dealt with the right of the municipality to expect to derive revenues from all of the buildings and structures within its bounds, whether they be owned privately or publicly. 1 ask the minister to respond if he would agree. By doing so, the minister will save me from going through a long series of questions in the committee if he could respond or even hear what 1 am saying with regard to one clause of the bill which befuddles me. I do not understand why it says in clause 2(2)(&):
except where otherwise prescribed, any real property leased to or occupied by a person or a body, whether incorporated or not, that is not a department
is exempt. 1 do not see how it fits and I do not know how it could be interpreted because it is open to such wide interpretation. If the minister could take a moment and look at that clause, perhaps in his closing remarks, if he intends to make any, he might address himself to what exactly that means. That gives considerable power, to the minister and to the Crown, power to rule out many of the things that may well have been included in some of the preceding sections.
As other members have said, and it is a point 1 meant to make on rising that I did not make, there is a tendency on the part of everyone-I share it as much as anyone else-to feel somewhat elated at the train of events and the obvious victory of the No forces in the province of Quebec this evening. However, I do want to offer a caution. The caution is this: there were a very large number of people in the province of Quebec tonight who voted Yes. We must, therefore, make an extra special effort to find out what it is about the federal system which has made those people feel that it would be appropriate for Quebec to have a degree of sovereignty, if not total sovereignty. 1 applaud the No side, and 1 supported it all the way through, but 1 am going to suggest that we must be very cautious. When 40 per cent of any group are so dissatisfied as to opt for the Yes side of the question, that is Yes to separation, then there is something dramatically wrong.

I also want to say to the minister that he should bear in mind that such things as conveyor belts and conveyance systems should be given careful consideration. As he well knows, they are used extensively in the mining industry. It is entirely possible that they are the only valuable part of the development that takes place. To exempt them under a piece of legislation such as this really does not make a lot of sense for some northern communities in which they might be situated. If the minister could give some thought to these few comments, 1 could feel better about the bill in general.

Mr. Speaker, I suppose we all realize that the eyes of the nation are not upon us this evening, but 1 am sure we all rejoice in the results that we are watching over television; 60 per cent for the No and 40 per cent for the Yes. I think the caution mentioned by the member from the NDP who just resumed his seat about the 40 per cent who are discontented has to be borne in mind. There can be no further delay in coming to grips with the problems of this country.
It is appropriate, nonetheless, that we should be discussing this bill tonight. It is one of those bills that ought to have been dealt with many, many moons ago. I understand this is the third time it has been before this House. Had it been dealt with earlier and been given a higher priority, it is quite possible that that 40 per cent would have been even lower, because we are dealing with something that is very close to the people who have to pay municipal taxes and those who run the municipalities, the mayors and the councillors. Therefore, while we may not be the main focus of attention this evening, we are dealing with a matter which is fundamental to the issue that is being determined now in the province of Quebec.

sula. The forest products laboratory is also a federal institution, as is the airport, the experimental farm, and the Work Point barracks.
All of these occupy lands in one or the other of the five municipalities which comprise the riding of Esquimalt-Saanich. Therefore, the municipal authorities in my area are very, very much reliant upon the grants in lieu taxes that are paid into the municipal treasuries for the financing of municipal works.
Royal Roads used to be in my riding, a magnificent park, now the Western College, a military college for all services, which held its graduating ceremonies only last week end. That is an unorganized territory.
There are one or two matters related to this bill that I feel I ought to bring to the minister's attention. One of them has been the delays that have occurred in the payments of the grants in lieu of taxes. On more than one occasion I have had to make representations to one department or another because the municipality has been in touch with me, frantically indicating that it was notified nine months ago that the grants were due and there had been no sign whatsoever of those grants showing up. The bills still keep rolling into the municipalities inevitably. Therefore, while this is a more generous extension of grants in lieu of taxes, I hope that this other matter, not just the generosity but the timeliness of the payments, will be taken into account by the minister. 1 hope 1 can get that assurance from him when he stands up to conclude debate on this bill.
The grants in lieu of taxes, of course, have their historic origins, as was mentioned by the previous speaker, with the Crown at one time being exempt from taxes. Gradually the municipalities are catching up on the Crown and this is the next stage in that catch-up, so to speak. Perhaps the time will come one day when municipal establishments will be paid the same assessment for the property that is occupied as any ordinary institution would pay.
It is sometimes difficult to make a comparison except perhaps on the basis of square feet, square yards, square hectares, square metres, or whatever will be used, between an airport and a business establishment such as a warehouse. There just is no comparison. However, 1 think a formula can be worked out so that the municipalities feel they are getting a fair deal.
This brings me to the question of assessments. An extraordinary situation was brought to my attention within the last two or three weeks which 1 would like to mention to the minister. 1 have written to one of his colleagues. It might be useful if 1 would send a copy of my letter to the minister, because there is an unusual relationship being built up by municipal assessors or regional district assessors. In this particular case, a private property is claiming a farm rate of assessment. The assessor is seeking a waiver to his income tax returns so that the regional district may have access to those returns in order to assure themselves that the statements in so far as the individual being assessed is concerned make him eligible for the farm rate of taxation.
I am sure the minister would not want this practice to go very far. I hope he would not. As far as I am concerned, and I hope as far as he is concerned, the income tax returns of the citizens of this country are a matter of confidentiality between those who submit the returns and the Department of National Revenue. However, as I get the story, the regional district assessor is doing his utmost to secure this waiver from the person being assessed. I do not know under what authority he can do that. I hope he will be appropriately reprimanded by the authorities who sent him out in the first place.
To my way of thinking, that person should be able to submit an affidavit to say that his income from the farm that he claims to be running is X number of dollars. That should be enough to guarantee his eligibility for a farm assessment rather than a residential assessment. If the assessor is not satisfied with the affidavit, then he should question it in the courts. The individual being assessed would then be able to prove by extracting a certain section from his income tax documents, if necessary, but not to open up his whole income tax return to any municipal authority.
I hope the minister agrees with me on the basis of stories I have given to him that that is a very improper practice for any authority to engage in and that, when he gets the information which I should be able to send him within the next day or so, he will be in a position to assure me that this is a practice which is certainly not acceptable to the government. So my first comment concerns the delay, and the desirability of an assurance from the minister that greater promptness will be forthcoming. I believe we should provide for an automatic triggering mechanism at a certain period of the year which municipalities can count on to ensure receipt of their grants in lieu of taxes without fail, year after year. I should like to see such a provision written into the bill, even through 1 am not sure whether that would be possible. We might examine in committee, whether there is a means of introducing into the bill an amendment establishing a date on which grants in lieu of taxes would be paid out to the municipalities. That is the first point.
The other point I underlined had to do with the abuse by a regional district authority in requiring a person being assessed to release his income tax returns to the regional district so that the officials concerned could reassure themselves because they were not prepared to take an individual's word that he was entitled to a farm rating rather than to a residential rating.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to address myself much more briefly than my last comments to Bill C-13. In my opinion this matter is one of housekeeping. It is a matter which ought not to engage a long debate in this House, and I would like to give my reasons why 1 offer that opinion and view.
A number of departments and agencies which are subject to statutory requirement to have offices or perform functions in Ottawa have relocated or are in the process of relocating outside the city of Ottawa. The situation must be rectified by new legislation which introduces changes in existing legislation covering each of the affected bodies to permit a legal recognition of the location of that agency or service outside the city of Ottawa. That is what the bill is about. It is a simple housekeeping matter. Bill C-13 deals with the necessary changes.
May 20, 1980

In five cases the words "City of Ottawa" are replaced by the words "National Capital Region". In the case dealing with the Department of Veterans Affairs moving to the city of Charlottetown, the words "City of Ottawa" are replaced by the words "such place in Canada designated by the governor in council". The location within the city of Charlottetown is a point of some concern to some members in the House, and I understand that the matter will be brought up in the late show tonight, Mr. Speaker.
Bills were introduced by the former ministers of public works in the previous two Parliaments to correct this situation, as was the case with Bill C-4 with which we dealt previously today. Bill C-13 is identical to Bill C-22 which was introduced on November 6, 1979, in the first session of the last Parliament, and which was the successor to Bill C-32 and Bill C-23 in the third and fourth sessions of the previous Parliament under the former Liberal government. To a municipal politician that means that people have gone through two elections and the bill is still sitting here.
A majority of these bodies which have been relocated during the past year or two are located in the national capital region, in Hull or Vanier. The affected bodies are the Economic Council of Canada, the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the Land Titles Office, the Canadian Transport Commission, Public Archives and DREE. In addition, provision is made for the relocation of the Canadian Pension Commission, the Pension Review Board, and the Department of Veterans Affairs to which l have referred.
The present bill, which is identical to Bill C-22, differs from Bill C-23 in that all references to the Farm Credit Corporation have been deleted. This change was introduced following the last government's decision in July of 1979 not to relocate to Camrose, Alberta, and it was deemed appropriate not to include it in the present legislation because of the uncertainty of a review of the over-all decentralization program.
In brief, that is the introduction of the bill.

me that the question of the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) was most relevant, because one of the things the taxpayers want to know, when you relocate an agency or a government department for whatever cause, be it good, bad, or political, is what is the cost to the taxpayer.
There are several matters which give us concern, and I must say that the minister, in the schizophrenic world in which we live in the political arena, perhaps chose well to put before us Bill C-4 first, and chose well when he decided to cut his parliamentary eye teeth on that bill, because Bill C-13 is a decayed and diseased wisdom tooth which should be extracted, because it has none of the parliamentary attributes of a positive nature that Bill C-4 had.
Here 1 want to digress for a minute because I know the minister ad libbed very well in his concluding remarks on Bill C-4 about the results of the vote tonight. I will not digress too far on the implications of that vote because others in other places tonight are perhaps trying to assess and divine the situation and the full implications of that vote. All I can say, having been a member here for a few years, is that 1 do not think the vote tonight has settled anything. I quite agree with those members of the House, as well as those who have spoken outside, that unless this House gets off the dead centre on many issues, some of the divining going on tonight may not be quite as prophetic and may perhaps be a little more pathetic than some people who believe in the federal system would like to believe.
1 do not feel any great excitement about the result tonight, although 1 am glad that the forces in favour of No have so obviously won. But when you get such a massive support for the Yes side, there are implications for any federal member who looks at the federal scene, let alone the disquiet and alienation in other parts of the country.
For a long time this House has been preoccupied with a justification for the problems in Quebec which is very close to us, especially when we talk about the national capital district. In fact there are those of us who could suggest, in terms of the history of Bill C-13, that now that the buildings are across the river in Quebec, in Hull, the government brings in what the minister euphemistically calls housekeeping legislation to legitimize retroactively the move of many departments across the river to the national capital region in Hull. Without getting too philosophical, I think Bill C-13 respecting the relocation of government agencies, in its strictest sense is involved in an indirect manner with the vote tonight.
As the minister mentioned, this matter is not new. We in this House saw changes in the Ottawa region, the capital region and/or construction on both sides of the river, without any great parliamentary debate. With the shift of locations of government agencies, now we are coming in to ensure, in the subject matters which the minister mentioned, be it the Economic Council of Canada, the Land Titles Act, the National Transportation Act, the Public Archives Act or the Department of Regional Economic Expansion Act, that where "Ottawa" appears it comes to mean "the national capital region."
There are two matters raised by Bill C-13, as far as 1 am concerned. One is the historic reason why we even have a Bill C-13, that is, expansion. I am not necessarily saying that I am against that, because it is a fact of life. A man called John Diefenbaker, a former leader of my party, in 1958 expanded the whole definition of the national capital region to include parts that were never included after many years. As your Honour knows, he expanded it far across the river. I do not want anyone to misinterpret my remarks tonight, but he expanded the definition of the national capital region to include other parts of the Ottawa area, the Ottawa-Hull area, the parkway system and the Gatineau. As the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) said, it is a pleasure for many of us who live here temporarily, or for those residents who live here permanently. It has enhanced the area. There is no resident of Ottawa or member of Parliament who has been here for a few years who has not seen the improvement in the national capital region.
Having said that on the positive side, through enhancement, enrichment and development in a positive sense of a national capital region, I cannot stand idly by, meekly bow, and say that we should now just acquiesce in retroactive approval of things which should have been debated in the House before they ever occurred. I am referring to the move of many agencies across the river into buildings there, leaving vacant space in the heart of Ottawa, let alone other moves across the country that have caused concern.
The minister may be a little surprised by my comment because I am from one of the so-called areas of economic disparity. It is not that so-called in economic terms. It is an area that is somewhat economically deprived. Having been in theory and in principle in favour of decentralization, I am sure the minister may wonder why this member for Atlantic Canada is questioning the principle in this bill of decentralization.

speechtext:
The answer to the rhetorical question and/or the question of the hon. member opposite, is that there is a real fundamental difference between decentralization in principle based on proper criteria and decentralization which occurs strictly for political patronage. As far as 1 am concerned. Bill C-13 is founded not only on weak history. It should have been debated, and perhaps it would not have caused the negative reaction in my mind. It should have come into the House open-ended. We talk about freedom of information and all the other things that members of Parliament and the public should be exposed to and know about, yet a case could be made for almost a surreptitious movement which in effect is legitimized, after the move, by bills such as Bill C-13.
I hope, when I speak this way, that future governments will not take this back-door approach to expand the operations of the federal government for whatever purpose, be it laudable or otherwise. This afternoon the minister did not answer any questions on Bill C-4 which were put objectively by members
May 20, 1980

on this side. Frankly, the questions were not that pointed because the members were all in favour of the principle of the bill which they kicked around. Ironically we have here a bill legitimizing "national capital region" for the word "Ottawa" for five government agencies in areas where the public servants have already moved in large measure, yet the bill has not moved off dead centre of the House of Commons. If the barn door has ever been closed after the cattle have gone out to pasture and were likely to break down the fence, Bill C-13 does it.
1 suggest that this bill must be looked at critically. One of the main reasons why it must be looked at especially critically now, notwithstanding the fact that tonight there was a very profound and historic vote in Quebec which has been good for the nation from sea to sea, is that tomorrow the work really begins. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and all party leaders in all parts of Canada must get down to discussing the merits and demerits of a renewed federalism and/or a renewed constitution. As some political scientists have said, there can be a real difference between a renewed constitution fundamentally or a brand new constitution fundamentally and a renewed federalism where parts of the whole, for example the provinces, have a much more meaningful say than perhaps they have had heretofore. I must say that I am somewhere in the middle, which perhaps is the safe place to be on a question like this.
I do not think the provinces are given a real meaningful say in a substantive way by just building buildings in different plots of land, no matter how great the building, no matter how great the plot. That type of cement mentality somehow often builds walls around the way we think about our federalism. We think it is there because of dollar signs.
From a personal point of view and that of a federal politician, albeit outside of the province of Quebec, I suggested this was a question for Quebec, although it affected all of Canada, because until very recently there was no emotional content in the debate in Quebec for those in favour of a No vote. I will not go much farther down that road, paying compliments where perhaps compliments can be paid. I might surprise some members in terms of where 1 think compliments should be paid. But 1 think the vote justifies the work of all who worked actively in the debate in Quebec. I hope we do not just stay on a Bill C-13 mentality, without substantive criteria for relocating agencies of government departments.
I am a politician and I make no apology for using the phrase "crass politics", but 1 must say that in terms not only of alienation of the regions of this country but also of the people of this land against politics, not only can they look at Bill C-13 and its strictness in terms of the national capital region in Ottawa, but they can look at what happened to the hon. member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) versus the former mayor of Cornwall.
Some people in the House do not yet know that the change of the Parks Commission from Cornwall to Peterborough followed the change from Cornwall to Quebec in order to divide the whole thing up. At one time the parks department
Decentralization
was solely in Cornwall and it looked after the interests of both Quebec and Ontario. When the parks department changed its location to Quebec in order to be closer to the people, naturally there was pressure to make sure that the remaining parks office in Cornwall was moved to where it could better serve the people of Ontario, where the park was, closer to Peterborough than Cornwall. It was not the Conservative government of a few months ago that suggested this. This is where the question of the hon. member for Yukon is most relevant. What is this topsyturvy flip-flop on parks in Cornwall or Peterborough, or the Charlottetown move, or the move of Eldorado from Port Hope to the northern Ontario region?
If there are legitimate reasons for this, when are we as politicians, or when is the government as the leader of politicians, i.e. the leader of this Parliament, going to start taking people into its confidence by saying, "Okay, there are five good reasons for the move and three bad ones, but these are best"? The people of Canada should make their choice, and those are the reasons. Sometime they will be able to make their choice.
There are many times as a member of Parliament, whether dealing with Bill C-13 which is trying to legitimize something which has occurred after the event, for example relocation, or another bill, I really cannot see the justification. This bill is trying to legitimize the move to a wider national capital from the narrow strict definition of Ottawa, that is, a relocation of government activities to other parts of the country under the umbrella of decentralization. I really wonder how you justify the move, for instance, to Peterborough from Cornwall.
I thought the whole concept of decentralization began with a move out of Ottawa to the periphery, the east and the west, or even to Winnipeg. 1 thought it was a move of activity out of Ontario, perhaps. I am talking as an Atlantic politician, and I feel there might be a little more benefit in a federal presence in areas more distant from Ottawa. However, we all know that decentralization has been manipulated and used for political purposes. As a politician I recognize the reality of that.
If politicians are to earn the respect of the alienated public out there from coast to coast, in contrast to alienated parts of the country, then the politicians in this chamber, especially the leaders here, i.e. the cabinet ministers, must have the intestinal fortitude to come clean.
This new Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove) has some experience in municipal politics in the Toronto area. 1 do not know the mechanics of the bylaws in the Scarborough region, but 1 know he was involved in municipal politics before becoming a federal member, and I am sure that he knows in most cases the workings of school boards and municipal councils at the grassroots level are more open and more public that here at the top of the totem pole.
1 am really serious that in areas where the public dollar is involved it is time we, as politicians, remember that we are not just playing the Parliament game under the rules of John A. Macdonald, and we all have to vote with the party whip-that

May 20, 1980
Decentralization
is a subject 1 would like to make a speech on at some time- but we are dealing with an alienated public not restricted just to Quebec. As a body corporate, as a House of Commons, if we make these moves we should make them for legitimate reasons.
Quite frankly I was not overly excited about confirming the move of the Department of Veterans Affairs to Charlottetown. I received briefs from legions of this land and talked to many good veterans who, quite frankly, were not excited about this move. I am speaking as an Atlantic member, talking about a move to Atlantic Canada which might help Atlantic Canada in terms of jobs, but there should be a good reason for such a move. I suggest in some areas the reasons should have been openly questioned with the merits and demerits placed on the table.
As far as I am concerned, as the lead-off speaker for my party in respect of Bill C-13, obviously the national capital is an area that has the approval and approbation of this side of the House. However, we do have to be critical about legitimizing things after the fact.
There is another question that has not been covered by this bill. Perhaps it is not overly relevant. Under the British North America Act, section 16, the capital of Canada shall be Ottawa until otherwise directed by order of the Queen's Council. As a result of these decentralization moves there may be people at the grassroots level who could successfully challenge the federal government. Some of these people may successfully challenge the federal government in respect of some of its regulations or laws having regard to some of these departments that have been carrying on business in certain areas for a couple of years. Perhaps an aggrieved citizen could challenge the federal government by suggesting that a head office must be here in Ottawa.
The suggestion could be made that the federal government must issue its edicts, its summonses, its expropriations and whatever here in Ottawa, the designated capital of the country. Such an individual might suggest that the federal government is out of circuit and out of tune because its head office has to be here in Ottawa. Such a challenge could be made on the basis of the change from Ottawa to the national capital region. From the little 1 used to know about constitutional law I think there very well might be a good class action on the part of the taxpayers regarding some of the federal processes. Tonight, or whenever we pass this bill, we will legitimize this change.
Let me conclude, since others want to speak, by saying that this is a pretty poor way to run a railway, and it is an even poorer way, quite seriously, to run a government. If there is anything that the vote in Quebec should tell us, and quite frankly, that the vote during the last two elections in 18 months, does tell us, it is that there is an alienated public out there, not enamoured with politicians in general and with some politicians in particular. I hope this new minister does not become confined with just the bureaucratic knee-jerk reaction. 1 respect those bureaucrats around us as fundamental and necessary, but the problems of government, and this includes
many political shades of government, occur when there is a knee-jerk reaction as a result of the advice of the bureaucracy.
I am informed that in regard to Bill C-4 there was a gentleman in the Department of Finance who has been involved in writing this proposed legislation with each change of Parliament, for about nine years. He has been involved in this legislation on grants in lieu of taxation to municipalities. He is obviously an expert. No doubt the answers the minister is provided for the questions that might be raised in the House by the opposition are good answers, but I hope this minister does not rely solely on the advice of these bureaucrats but, rather, takes advantage of the experience he has had in the municipal field.
I hope he uses his newness in this government, which is an old government, when looking at some of these problems with a fresh approach. Perhaps in this way he can avoid any further deterioration of the public's respect for the political process, and that deterioration has occurred from coast to coast, regardless of region. Hopefully in this way we can avoid a repetition of some of the dramatic events which have occurred in this country. 1 am sure we will be faced with even greater problems in the future as we go on with the nation's business in a substantive way. I would hope, therefore, when the minister concludes his remarks in this debate, or when providing information in the committee, he will make sure there are answers to the questions, including those asked by the hon. member for Yukon earlier regarding two precise points.
The minister could bring in those figures tomorrow. With the answers to these questions and those figures, this debate might be expedited. In this way he could perhaps cast bread on the waters and ease the passage of the bill. Whether this information comes tomorrow or at the committee, members of Parliament on all sides, and especially ministers, have an extra duty to be more open than the government certainly has been. Until that takes place we will just be whistling Dixie if we think the public is going to have a different perception of politicians who are supposed to be running this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO RELOCATE GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to speak to Bill C-13 this evening. It is a privilege to speak on this day, particularly in light of the results which have been realized tonight in la belle province. I would like to congratulate the minister, the hon. member for York-Scarbor-ough (Mr. Cosgrove), on his dynamic approach to his responsibilities. With the introduction of both Bill C-4 and Bill C-13 in the same day, he is obviously a very busy minister. 1 would like to identify and associate myself with this dynamic minister in the sense that I was able to relate to his remarks earlier this evening, having served personally on a municipal government for eight years in New Brunswick.
I speak in support of the relocation of the government agencies, but before 1 get into my remarks I would like to take this opportunity to participate in what I feel is true debate in this House between two members on such a bill. The previous
May 20, 1980

speaker, the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) contradicated himself so many times that he laid the groundwork on which 1 can say something about the importance of the relocation of government agencies to the Atlantic area.
The hon. member started off by saying that he would be brief, but then he went on for a long period of time holding up this bill. He mentioned the two elections and the fact that there has been a long delay in the passage of legislation in this House. From that comment, I understood the hon. member to mean that he was as anxious as all of us are to clean up these housekeeping bills and get on with the nation's business, as he called it. Yet, the hon. member went on to say a number of negative things about what the minister is attempting to do.
The very fact that the hon. member does come from the Atlantic area, and after saying what he said this evening, very clearly established the case that he was contradicting himself.
I do not know why the hon. member would do that, or from what base he made those remarks when he criticized the move to Prince Edward Island. This is a move which 1 have supported 100 per cent, not only in the days when we were in government but during the days, that very brief period of time, when we were in opposition. I defended the decision taken by our colleague, the former minister of veterans affairs, even when he was not here in the House. Now that he is back and is the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) again, he has the privilege of seeing the work he commenced in an earlier Parliament come into reality.
As one who had the privilege to serve as the parliamentary secretary to the then minister of urban affairs who was also responsible for CMHC and other matters, I had an opportunity to realize fully the workings of the National Capital Commission. I join with other members in stating my belief and understanding of the importance of the national capital. Of course I will not be able to muster the enthusiasm nor find the words to express how proud 1 am of the nation's capital and of Ottawa, but 1 have nothing but admiration and understanding for the work and the role of the members who represent this region.
1 state that because as a member of Parliament 1 understand the difficulties of those members of Parliament, and 1 sympathize with them as representatives of the people of this region. On the other hand, it being a two-way street, I would hope that they would understand our position, coming from a have-not, underdeveloped region of the country.
There is very little which I can add this evening in this debate. It has been so well stated by our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on previous occasions and, more recently now that we have commenced with a new administration, that both he and the government have indicated how strongly they hold the position that the have provinces must continue to seek and to find ways and means to assist in every way the have-not and underdeveloped areas.
That is why I find it strange for a member from the Atlantic provinces, the member from Annapolis Valley, to stand in his place and qualify himself eminently as a member speaking out
Decentralization
of both sides of his mouth. On the one hand he said that we may need this type of relocation and support for the Atlantic area and, on the other hand, he chastised the government, by bringing in the usual type of sly innuendo, that decisions were taken for other than appropriate reasons.
The program which was announced in October, 1977, addressed the relocation of several thousands of full and part-time jobs from the capital area to 24 communities in all ten provinces between the period of 1977 to 1982. I will make no reservations about it since I represent an important constituency in New Brunswick. 1 am very much interested in supporting Bill C-13 this evening because I want to do what 1 can in my work to attract some relocation of government agencies to my area, which is one of the most beautiful areas in Canada. I refer to the beautiful Restigouche River, the salmon and all that we have going into the Gaspe area.
However, we also need jobs in order to survive, and we must develop the economy. We have some industry there with mines, with the Noranda group and Bathurst Mining and Smelting. We have the pulp and paper industry which employs thousands of Canadians who are hard-working people. There is also tourism and various other aspects which will help the economy. However, we also need due and fair consideration when it comes to relocation and decentralization.

Mr. Speaker, given the events of earlier this evening, I must join with all of those who tonight will not necessarily breathe a sigh of relief because well in excess of one million of our fellow Canadians have expressed a desire that may not be in sympathy with our own, while slightly less than two million have expressed the opposite desire. 1 do not think we should take any comfort from that. It is clear that we have an extraordinary task ahead of us to reunite this country.
In terms of the question that 1 raised on April 17 having to do with energy, how we are going to pay for it and how we are going to bring it into this country, might 1 raise two points for the distinguished parliamentary secretary whom I do not see here at the moment but who, 1 hope, is here. These two questions have to do with the rejection this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) of any possibility of participation by Canadians and Canadian ships crewed by Canadians and subject to Canadian law in the movement of energy from Mexico into Canada.
This afternoon the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us that the question, to the besLof his knowledge, has not
even been raised. In such a vital area to Canada, I am amazed that the question has not even been raised.
Last year leaving ourselves open to external interests, as Canadians we paid very close to $3.7 billion on the movement of goods in and out of this country by water-borne means. That includes exports overland of Canadian manufactured goods, through the United States, exporting through United States ports. These goods went out in foreign-registered bottoms, not Canadian ships, but foreign registered ones. The agencies here in Canada took their usual fees for these purposes, but the ships were foreign registered.
In discussions with Mexico with respect to the agreement to import eventually upwards of 100,000 barrels of oil a day into Canada-and I speak as an eastern Canadian who is totally reliant on imported oil-1 am told this afternoon by the government of this country that the question of who would move that oil was not even considered. I find that reprehensible. 1 find it equally reprehensible with respect to energy and the question of whether or not this government has bothered to consider how we are going to export northeastern British Columbia coal to Japan.
It is my suspicion, not confirmed and not too late to be corrected, that this government has not even introduced into its discussions the possibility of the utilization of Canadian ships built in Canada, crewed by Canadians and subject to Canadian law, in the export of Canadian natural resources to Japan. It is my suspicion that that has not even happened.
A second problem that I raised on April 17 had to do with where the money is to come from to pay for eastern oil in terms of compensation. It is not in anything mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). In fact it is some $2.5 billion to $2.8 billion short of the premises on which the Minister of Finance introduced his mini-budget. I am sorry to see only one member of the Treasury Bench here, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove). 1 am pleased he is here this evening. Where is the money going to come from? How is the money going to be raised to meet that compensation fund? 1 want an answer to that question.
The third question I posed on April 17 had to do with whether the government was prepared to honour the commitment given by the previous government to assist refineries in eastern Canada with regard to the upgrading of their facilities in order to accommodate the heavier crudes now coming out of Venezuela and which will come out of Mexico. Where will the money come from to help them? Are they going to have to do it on their own? If so, when will they be told so that they may start on their own? If there is any federal financial assistance forthcoming, when will they know about it? When will they know what the level of assistance will be?
Those are my three points. When in God's name are we going to start to move our own resources-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in raising this matter this evening the hon. member has provided the opportunity to demonstrate again the international involvement of this government in ensuring a stable and secure energy supply for Atlantic Canada.
Last week 1 indicated to the House what we have done to foster energy conservation and diversification in the maritime provinces. While those efforts have already brought rewards and shown considerable further promise, we cannot eliminate the need to import oil into Atlantic Canada in the immediate future.
An energy agreement with one foreign supplier, Mexico, was initialed in May, 1979, one year ago. It provides for the delivery of Mexican crude oil to Canada. The intent is to initiate delivery this year, increasing to 50,000 barrels per day one year after delivery commences. Later, if Mexican production allows, this may rise to a volume of 100,000 barrels per day. The precise mix of heavy and light crude oil remains to be negotiated.
As is the case elsewhere in the world, eastern Canadian refineries have a limited capacity to process heavy oil. Certainly we have a responsibility to consider these limitations while negotiating with Mexico. Once this oil supply agreement is finalized, Petro-Canada is expected to arrange for the efficient transport of this oil to eastern Canadian destinations. We expect that this will minimize the costs involved, and allow Petro-Canada to exercise its mandate to assist in protecting our national interests. If available and suitable, we shall, of course, give first priority to Canadian ships.
While the price of Mexican crude is in the upper range of current international prices, it would be accepted by companies which look forward to receiving crude oil from a secure source. This acceptance can be explained by the fact that crude oil contracts from other sources would likely entail prices which would equal, or exceed, the price of Mexican crude available to Canada.
To respond to the subject the hon. member raised regarding financial assistance to the refining system, I can repeat that it was studied extensively in 1979 in consultation with officials from provincial governments, including those of Atlantic Canada. At that time it was concluded that no assistance would be required. Accordingly, the previous Conservative government took no steps to provide financial aid to those who would be refining imported Mexican crude oil.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-RELOCATION OE DVA SITE IN CHARLOTTETOWN
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-RELOCATION OE DVA SITE IN CHARLOTTETOWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this historic and happy occasion 1 hesitate to raise a mundane matter although the issue I wish to discuss is of great interest to my riding of Hillsborough, to my province of Prince Edward
Adjournment Debate
Island and, indeed, to all Canadians concerned about good government. It has to do with a question in the House of Commons on Tuesday, May 13, 1980, which, in the first instance, I put to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). It concerned the attempt by the federal government to locate the Department of Veterans Affairs in the centre of Charlottetown, the capital city of Prince Edward Island, despite a binding legal agreement between the federal government on the one hand and the province of Prince Edward Island and the city of Charlottetown on the other, through the Charlottetown Area Development Corporation. The agreement required the Department of Veterans Affairs to be located on the waterfront.
I asked the President of the Treasury Board on that occasion whether it was his intention and that of the government to ignore the obligations they had incurred under the binding agreement, and whether it was also the intention of the government to force its choice of site on the people of Prince Edward Island. The hon. gentleman was unable to answer my question, and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cosgrove), in an effort to rescue his colleague, entered the discussion and answered as best he could. In essence, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works presented more or less the same statement that he tabled the next day, an analysis on the basis of which the government proceeded with the change of site. Mr. Speaker, the answer to my question by the Minister of Public Works and the statement he tabled in the House the next day were both riddled with inaccuracies and unfounded assumptions. In the short time I have at my disposal in the House tonight, 1 would like to deal briefly with each of his points.
The first had to do with cost. He maintained that the waterfront site was between $1 million and $1.5 million more expensive than the uptown, alternative site. The truth is that the waterfront site is valued at $1.5 million. By contrast, the uptown site is valued at $2.1 million, leaving an advantage in favour of the waterfront site of $600,000. It is true, as the statement provided to this House by the Minister of Public Works pointed out, that piles and a seawall are required to be installed to make the waterfront site suitable for a massive federal government building. But the cost, according to the best estimates, would not exceed about $400,000, still leaving an advantage of something like $200,000 in favour of the waterfront site. But one has to calculate also the additional cost to the federal treasury of getting out of the binding agreement with the Charlottetown Area Development Corporation, which may exceed a million dollars. So it may well be that it will cost in excess of a million dollars for the federal government to change the site from the waterfront to the central core for political reasons.
The second point the minister made in his answer and, in his statement the next day, was the desirability of the uptown site compared with the waterfront location, in terms of parking, of traffic and of other things such as bringing business to the neighbouring retail stores. The truth is, Mr. Speaker, that the proposal for the uptown site does not even conform with the

May 20, 1980
Adjournment Debate
city's bylaws, guidelines, and restrictions with respect to the required ratio of parking spaces to the number of employees in a building.
What is more, the proposal to which the minister is a party would contemplate the placement of a massive federal government building right in the heart of a small community-a capital city but, nevertheless, a small community. This measure will worsen parking problems, especially in the summer, when we have something like 600,000 visitors. During that time of year, 600,000 tourists are added to the population of Prince Edward Island, which is only 123,000. The uptown site will cause congestion of traffic in the centre area of the city, and it will devour valuable commercial space better suited to commercial purposes rather than government or institutional purposes.
Almost as important, I think, is that the decision will place a huge federal government building across the street from the provincial legislature, which is a national historic site. The building is a shrine because it was where the Fathers of Confederation met in 1864 to draft the British North America Act. The placement of the building on the waterfront, on the other hand, would give a much needed boost to the waterfront development that is going on with the help of the federal government, the province and the city, and into which the federal government itself has already poured something like $5 million.
By changing the site and by wrenching out of that project the Department of Veterans Affairs, which was to be the centre-piece or flaghip of the waterfront development, the federal government has in effect undermined a project in which it itself is substantially involved.
I want to make one additional point in conclusion. The waterfront site is not, as was implied by the minister, a million miles away from the centre area. It is only three blocks from the downtown centre. It is close enough to the centre of the city to complement local businesses and retail outlets, while being far enough away not to disrupt city planning in the way the downtown core option would.
May I conclude by saying that the placement of the building in the centre core of the downtown area will not accelerate the relocation, as the minister implied. The fact is that with the haggling that will take place between the federal government and CADC over the binding agreement, and with so little done in the uptown core area by way of preparation, this change in site from the waterfront to the centre area will delay rather than accelerate the relocation of DVA to Charlottetown-

subtopic: TRANSPORT-CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
TRANSPORT-CROWSNEST PASS FREIGHT RATES- GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with regard to my question of May 15, which was followed by my question of privilege on May 16, I expressed my sympathy to the minister for having been misled by the Canadian Pacific Railway over the matter of CP rail's freezing of the $322 million Rogers Pass project until the government adjusted the Crowsnest Pass freight rate.
I offered sympathy because CP has sent the minister into the House stark naked except for the pathetic excuse that CP executive vice-president Bill Stinson had been misquoted when he had talked to five reporters on the special Calgary to Vancouver train which was showing off all the improvement CP was making to increase the capacity of its main line, but not all the improvements, however, because Mr. Stinson said that if the Crowsnest rate was not replaced by a compensatory rate of about five or six times as high, CP Rail would freeze Rogers Pass improvement as a sign of bad faith with the Government of Canada over the transport policy. That was Mr. Stinson's statement to the Canadian Press reporter, Steve Merdl. Then, one of CP Rail's highly paid public relations men no doubt told one of the assistants of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) that Mr. Stinson had been misquoted.
However, that was not the end of the story. Then the other reporters on the train started filing their stories. I have mentioned that one of them, Bobbi Lambright of the Edmonton Journal, filed an almost identical story to the Canadian Press account. Miss Lambright wrote, and I quote from her story in the Edmonton Journal of Thursday, May 15:
If the money-
May 20, 1980

That is, money from higher compensatory rates for hauling grain.
-is not available, some major projects will have to be shelved resulting in serious ramifications for rail transportation in the 1980s. A $300 million double tracking project through the Rogers Pass could be the main casualty if finances are not available.
The link between the Crowsnest Pass rate, which the CPR would dearly love to do away with, and the CPR main line improvements, was established by those reporters. This is what I was referring to when 1 said the CPR was practising corporate blackmail on the Government of Canada.
There was further evidence. The CBC has a reporter on this train to nowhere, and his report made the same link. Canadian Press, which is always sensitive to charges of misquotation, declined to change its story.
This was the background to our question on Thursday, May 1 5, and the subsequent question of privilege on Friday, May 16. On the question, I am sorry but the minister and this House have been shamed by the statement by CP Rail which has proved incorrect.
1 am somewhat more disturbed about the matter of privilege. Madam Speaker ruled stating that it appeared to her to be a matter of whether the MP was satisfied with the answer given by the minister. The question before the House was whether the House had been misled. If so, why whould CP rail not be called before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections to determine why they had decided to tell the minister something other than what three trained newspaper reporters had concluded after an extensive interview with executive vice-president Stinson?
There is a legitimate press issue here, Mr. Speaker. We are often confronted with a public figure who, when he has said something indiscreet, hides behind the protective veil of claiming he was misquoted. This does the press of this country, which already has serious credibility problems with its public, little good in establishing its own legitimacy as the reporter of public events which serves the vital function of shaping public opinion in this nation.
If this matter could have been cleared up by the committee, I think the press, the public and the Parliament of this nation would have been better served for it. That is my regret, Mr. Speaker.
Also, we could have returned in the House to the substance of my first inquiry, namely, whether it is the Government of Canada or CPR which determines the transportation policy in this country. Would the government invoke section 262 of the Railway Act if Mr. Stinson makes good on his threat to move grain at a lower priority than other freight if the Crow rate remains in place, thereby ensuring that western farmers get the priority they deserve in shipping the export wheat which does much to earn the foreign exchange which this country needs so desperately? Would the government consider the recommendations for Crow related freight rates as recommended in the Hall Commission report on grain handling and
Adjournment Debate
transportation, and remove the disparities for producers of semi-finished goods such as rapeseed meal and oil?
These are the real questions that matter in the west, not whether some functionary for the CPR claims he was misquoted. We should have an end to these kinds of diversionary tactics which impede the work of the House and its members. What we need are answers to the questions which are on the minds of many westerners, as they see what is supposed to be the fate of this country played out as in Quebec tonight.
I do not doubt that this is so, but I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bockstael) to come prepared with answers to this House when questions are asked. It is not an edifying experience to have to sit here and listen while the minister ducks a simple question as to whether the advisory committee of the Canadian Wheat Board was consulted when the initial price of wheat was set this year. Surely one of the minister's dedicated assistants could find that out with a simple telephone call to Winnipeg. If that kind of candor and dedication were more readily displayed, then there would be fewer questions of privilege coming before this House.
Now that the authenticity of the blackmail has been established, would the Minister of Transport answer my question: what does he intend to do in the face of this blackmail?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Dominion Government and the Canadian Pacific Railway entered into the Crowsnest Pass agreement in 1897. In return for certain concessions, the railway agreed to lower rail rates on grain and to maintain them at that level. The Crowsnest Pass rates were incorporated into the Railway Act in 1925. They now apply to western grain moving for export as well as domestic grain moving eastwards to Thunder Bay.
The low rates on grain began to make themselves felt in the 1950s, and the effect upon the railways was recognized by the MacPherson commission from 1959 to 1961. In 1975 the Snavely commission was appointed to identify the costs to the railways of moving grain at statutory rates. The Snavely commission found that the 1974 cost of moving grain was $231 million. Three years later, by 1977, the cost had risen to $354 million. In that same period the railways' share of the costs almost doubled from $89 million to $175.5 million. It is evident that the continued existence of the Crowsnest rate will exert a significant impact upon the finances of our two major railways. The impact of the statutory rate on other parties must not, however, be forgotten.
With respect to the position of Canadian Pacific's proposed $322 million Beavermouth, British Columbia, tunnel project, economic growth forecasts for western Canada in the 1980s will require a marked expansion of railway capacity to move traffic between Calgary, Edmonton and the west coast. While there is an ever-increasing demand for railway capacity, we

May 20, 1980
Adjournment Debate
arc all experiencing a very high inflation rate, which means for railways a very high capital cost for capacity additions. Until now the railways have been able to add capacity in relatively small increments such as dieselization, large capacity cars, and long trains. These methods have been exhausted, and now both CN and CP rail are faced with large, one-time plant capacity expansion programs through the mountains.
The railways have not been able to increase their revenues in relation to the increased requirement for funds. About 22 per cent of the total traffic handled through the Rockies by CP rail is grain which moves on a fixed rate. The minister has requested up-to-date forecasts for grain traffic and a report on
capacity expansion from the president of CN by this September. Also, CP Rail is expecting to provide the minister with information on its capacity expansion. With this information we will be able to deal with the important issue of the availability of railway capacity for western Canada.
The minister outlined his views on the Crow rate in the House during the debate on this subject on May 15, 1980, and I need not reiterate them here for the hon. member.
